# Prologue: two nights {.unnumbered}

Picture a shipping company's security team. Its computers raise a warning, called an **alert**, whenever something looks suspicious: a sign-in from a strange country, an email with an odd link, a laptop talking to an unknown server. Someone has to look at each alert and decide: real attack, or nothing?

Tonight one person is on duty. Checking an alert properly takes about twelve minutes, so they can check about five an hour.

![One night, midnight to 7 a.m. Each line is an alert; the real attacks are red, taller and marked on top. Working in the order they arrive, the person on duty checks the ones on the left. The rest wait for the morning.](/figures/front/night.pdf){#fig-night}

@fig-night shows the whole night. {{< num front night_alerts int >}} alerts arrived between midnight and seven. {{< num front night_threats int >}} of them were real attacks. Working through them in the order they arrived, the person on duty checked {{< num front night_opened int >}}, and only {{< num front night_threats_opened int >}} of those were real.

They made no mistakes. Every alert they checked, they judged correctly. The problem was the order. The queue decided what they looked at, and a queue only knows what arrived first.

Now picture a second night.

A model reads every alert the moment it arrives. It writes nothing. It answers one question with a number: *how likely is this to be real?* And that number can be trusted: of the alerts it calls "one in ten", about one in ten really are attacks.

Alerts it is almost sure are harmless get closed, and a random few of those are kept aside to be checked later. Alerts it is fairly sure are dangerous wake someone up at once. Everything in between goes to the person on duty, most likely first.

The person still makes the decisions that matter. They just make them on the right alerts.

That second night is what this book builds. It needs surprisingly little new technology and quite a lot of clear thinking:

- what a probability really is, and how to tell if one can be trusted;
- what each kind of mistake costs, and where that puts the line between "act" and "ignore";
- when a machine should decide, and when it should hand the case to a person.

None of this is only about security. The same thinking runs a bank's fraud check, a hospital's waiting list and every AI agent that has to choose its next step. The security team is just the example we'll keep coming back to, because its mistakes are easy to count.

::: {.nexthook}
Next: before a machine can decide anything, it has to learn. What does that actually mean?
:::
